<meta>continues from previous page: someone delights in the fiction itself; regarding whom it is said in the third book of the Ethics <note>Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics</note>, chapter 7, near the middle, that he seems more vain than evil; for the same reasoning applies to lying and simulation. It happens, however, sometimes that someone simulates a perfection of holiness which is not necessary for salvation; and such simulation is neither always a mortal sin, nor is it always accompanied by a mortal sin. And by this, the response to the objections is clear.</meta>

---

->QUESTION CXII<-

ON BOASTING. — Divided into two articles.

Next we must consider boasting — and irony, which are parts of lying, according to the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> in the fourth book of the Ethics, chapter 7.
First, regarding boasting, two things are asked: 1. to which virtue it is opposed; 2. whether it is a mortal sin.

->ARTICLE ONE<-

Whether boasting is opposed to the virtue of truth.

Regarding the first, we proceed as follows. 1. It seems that boasting is not opposed to the virtue of truth. For lying is opposed to truth. But sometimes there can be boasting even without a lie; as when someone shows off their own excellence: for it is said in Esther 1:3-4: *Ahasuerus made a great feast..., that he might show the riches of the glory of his kingdom* (1) *and the greatness and excellence of his power.* Therefore, boasting is not opposed to the virtue of truth.
2. Furthermore, boasting is listed by Gregory <note>Pope Gregory the Great</note> in the 23rd book of his Morals <note>Morals on Job</note>, chapter 4, near the beginning, as one of the four species of <term>superbia</term> <gloss>pride</gloss>, specifically when someone boasts that they have what they do not have; hence it is said in Jeremiah 48:29: *We have heard of the pride of Moab (he is exceeding proud), his loftiness, and his arrogance, and his pride, and the haughtiness of his heart. I know, says the Lord, his boasting, and that his power is not according to it.* And in the 31st book of the Morals, chapter 7, near the middle, Gregory says that boasting arises from <term>inanis gloria</term> <gloss>vainglory</gloss>. But pride and vainglory are opposed to the virtue of humility. Therefore, boasting is not opposed to truth, but to humility.

<margin>ARTICLE I. — Boasting properly so-called is a vice by which someone externally elevates themselves above what is within them. Although, according to the usage of the word, boasting may also be said of the display of truth beyond the opinion or knowledge of others, as a vice in its own category (for only thus is it properly understood), it is not spoken of except as the opposite of truth, by way of excess; for only in this way is it the name of a vice by its nature. For the display of truth beyond the knowledge of others is not evil by its nature, but is sometimes good according to necessity or utility, and sometimes evil because of a bad end (Cajetan <note>Thomas de Vio, a 16th-century commentator on Aquinas</note>).</margin>

(1) The Vulgate <note>The standard Latin Bible</note> reads: ...The riches of the glory of his kingdom.

<column-break/>

3. Furthermore, boasting seems to be caused by riches; hence it is said in Wisdom 5:8: *What has pride profited us, or what advantage has the boasting of riches brought us?* But the superfluity of riches seems to pertain to the sin of <term>avaritia</term> <gloss>greed/avarice</gloss>, which is opposed to justice or liberality. Therefore, boasting is not opposed to truth.
— But against this is what the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says in the second and fourth books of the Ethics, chapter 7, in both places (1) that boasting is opposed to truth.

I ANSWER that <term>jactantia</term> <gloss>boasting</gloss> seems properly to imply that a man extols himself in words. For those things which a man wishes to throw far <note>Latin: "jactare"</note>, he raises up high. A person properly extols himself when he says something about himself that is above himself. This happens in two ways: — sometimes a person speaks of himself, not indeed above what is in himself, but above what men think of him; which the Apostle <note>St. Paul</note> avoiding, says in 2 Corinthians 12:6: *I forbear, lest any man should think of me above that which he sees in me, or anything he hears from me.* — In another way, someone extols himself through words, speaking of himself above what is in himself according to the truth of the matter. And because a person should be judged more according to what is in himself than according to what is in the opinion of others, it is for this reason that it is more properly called boasting when someone elevates himself above what is in himself than when he elevates himself above what is in the opinion of others; although in both ways it can be called boasting. And therefore **boasting properly so-called is opposed to truth by way of excess.**

To the first, therefore, it must be said that the argument proceeds regarding boasting insofar as it exceeds opinion.
To the second, it must be said that the sin of boasting can be considered in two ways: — in one way according to the species of the act, and thus it is opposed to truth, as was said in the body of the article and in Question 110, Article 2; — in another way according to its cause, from which, although not always, it nevertheless more frequently happens; and thus it proceeds indeed from pride as from an internal motivating and impelling cause. For from the fact that someone is internally elevated above themselves through arrogance, it usually follows that they boast of greater things about themselves externally, although sometimes someone proceeds to boasting not from arrogance, but from a certain vanity, and delights in this, because such is their habit. And therefore <term>arrogantia</term> <gloss>arrogance</gloss>, through which someone is extolled above themselves, is a species of pride; yet it is not the same as boasting, but is more frequently its cause. And for this reason Gregory places boasting among the species of pride. Moreover, the boaster usually tends toward achieving glory through his boasting; and therefore, according to Gregory, it arises from vainglory according to the reason of the end.

(1) In the edition of Nicolas, the word "in both places" is missing.

<summary>This page discusses the vice of boasting, defining it as the act of exalting oneself through words beyond reality or common opinion. Aquinas concludes that boasting is primarily a sin against the virtue of truth because it involves an excess of self-representation.</summary>
<keywords>boasting, jactantia, truth, pride, vainglory, arrogance, Aristotle, Gregory the Great, Aquinas, Ethics</keywords>
